workloads.name: SAXPY (vector update)
workloads.what: Updates a long vector with y = a·x + y: almost pure memory traffic.

header.achieved: At sizes larger than the cache: 416 GB/s to 418 GB/s (76% of the theoretical limit); best at size 2^25, fp64.
why: Each element is read and written once with almost no arithmetic, so memory speed sets the limit; sizes that fit in the cache can run faster than memory allows.

workloads.name: Sparse matrix × vector (SpMV)
workloads.what: Multiplies a matrix that is mostly zeros by a vector, as used in scientific solvers.

header.achieved: At sizes larger than the cache: 165 GB/s to 394 GB/s (30–72% of the theoretical limit); best at size 16384, density 0.25, fp32.
why: Mostly streams the matrix from memory; the irregular (power-law) matrix reads the vector at scattered places, which wastes part of the memory bandwidth.

workloads.name: Sparse matrix × matrix (SpGEMM)
workloads.what: Multiplies two mostly-zero matrices, as used in graph analytics.

peak: No single hardware limit applies: building a sparse result needs scattered memory accesses, so results are reported in GB/s.
header.achieved: Reached 0.28 GB/s to 21.2 GB/s across sizes; best at size 4096, density 0.01, fp64.
why: Building a sparse result needs scattered memory accesses and bookkeeping, so it reaches only a small share of the memory limit on every machine.

workloads.name: Matrix multiply (GEMM)
workloads.what: Multiplies two dense square matrices: the core operation of scientific computing and AI.

peak: Compute: 3584 cores × 2 × 1.30 GHz boost = 9.3 TFLOP/s fp32; fp64 4.7
header.achieved: Reached 1.8 TFLOP/s to 8.6 TFLOP/s across sizes (38–92% of the theoretical limit); best at size 8192, fp32.
why: Matrix multiply reuses each value many times, so large matrices run close to the compute limit; small matrices are held back by start-up overhead.

workloads.name: Matrix × vector (GEMV)
workloads.what: Multiplies a dense matrix by a vector (an earlier benchmark, not one of the 16 final workloads).

header.achieved: At sizes larger than the cache: 98.8 GB/s to 411 GB/s (18–75% of the theoretical limit); best at size 2048, fp64.
why: Each matrix value is used exactly once, so memory speed sets the limit; small sizes fit in the cache.
